Build, buy, partner or open source

What must we build ourselves, and what should we buy or borrow? A near-expert treatment of the sourcing decision, worked through two companies, one 36-month horizon and the arithmetic that most decision memos never do.

1Two decisions, ten days apart

On Monday 5 October 2026, Nachiket Hirlekar sat with a printout he had asked his team not to circulate. Vriksha Life Insurance writes 38,000 new life proposals a month, carries 11.2 lakh policies in force and manages ₹3,180 crore of policyholder assets from Pune. Each proposal arrives with medical reports, bank statements, income proofs and identity documents — an average of 7.4 files. A nine-week time-and-motion study put the handling cost of one proposal at 14.5 minutes of underwriting-operations time. At 38,000 proposals that is 5,51,000 minutes, or 9,183.33 hours, a month; at Vriksha's loaded operations rate of ₹310 an hour, ₹28.47 lakh a month.

A pilot on 2,400 proposals had cut average handling to 6.2 minutes by extracting most structured fields without a human touch. Held at 38,000 proposals, that is 2,35,600 minutes, or 3,926.67 hours, or ₹12.17 lakh a month — a saving of ₹16.30 lakh a month. Two engineers had assembled the pilot in three weeks using open-weight models. Nachiket's printout listed four ways to productionise it: buy a platform from Vyavastha Document Intelligence, self-host an open-source and open-weight stack, hand intake to Vishranti Claims Services on a per-proposal fee, or build from first principles. His chief risk officer, Naveena Hampiholi, had told him that whichever he chose, the IRDAI outsourcing framework would leave accountability on Vriksha's board.

Ten days later, on Thursday 15 October, Nirupama Hazarika faced a decision that looked identical and behaved nothing like it. Vedhan Retail Cloud sells a hosted storefront to 1,100 merchants from Bengaluru and serves 3.00 crore search queries a month, growing at 3.5 per cent a month. Search is the largest driver of its merchants' conversion and the loudest item in its churn interviews. Her platform lead, Nikhil Hanamsagar, wanted to self-host OpenSearch and write Vedhan's own ranking layer; her CFO, Nilanjana Hazare, wanted a managed vendor. A specialist firm had offered a white-label arrangement at six per cent of search-attributed revenue, which Nandita Hubballi, who runs merchant success, thought obviously right because it carried almost no capital.

Both decisions run over the same 36 months, 1 November 2026 to 31 October 2029, which is why they can be compared at all. The argument this page builds is that the four-box framing is almost always applied at the wrong unit of analysis, on the wrong horizon, with the wrong cost base — and that once those errors are corrected, the interesting decision is rarely which box to tick.

2The idea, and who disagrees about it

Define the decision precisely. For a given component of a product — not a capability, not a feature area, but a unit with an interface you could describe in a paragraph — the sourcing decision is the choice of production mode: build (produce it with your own people under your own direction), buy (acquire it as a priced good or service under contract), partner (obtain it through a relationship whose terms are partly non-contractual and whose consideration is often a share of outcome), or open source (take it from a commons under a licence and assume the operating obligations yourself). The last is not a cheap kind of buying but a distinct mode of production: nothing to pay, nobody to call, and a maintenance liability that begins the day you deploy.

The question was invented to solve a boundary problem. Ronald Coase, in 1937, asked why firms exist at all if markets allocate efficiently, and answered that using a market has costs — finding a supplier, negotiating, enforcing — so activity moves inside the firm when those exceed the cost of managing it internally. Oliver Williamson made this operational by naming the attributes that make exchange expensive: asset specificity (how useless the investment is to anyone else), uncertainty and frequency. Where specificity is high, supplier and buyer are locked together, each can hold the other up, and contracts cannot cover the contingencies — so you integrate.

Modularity and options (Baldwin and Clark, Design Rules, 2000; Christensen) Sourcing is downstream of architecture; defining the interface is itself the strategic act. Integrate across whatever interface is not yet good enough. That the profitable boundary is stable — modularity creates options whose value moves with technology.
Commons-based peer production (Benkler; von Hippel) Open source is a third mode of production, governed by the health of its contributor community, not by its licence price. That open source is the default on cost grounds — its own literature on unmaintained critical infrastructure refutes that.

3Mechanics in depth

Expert practice has three moves, all usually left implicit. First, decomposition: refuse to source a capability; insist on components with interfaces. Second, horizon and base discipline: fix one horizon, one scope and one team, and force every column onto it. Third, pricing the exit before signing the entry. Take the second first, because it is where memos break.

Nirupama fixed the horizon at the 36 months from 1 November 2026 and the scope at the index and retrieval component — query in, result set out, with autocomplete and merchandising rules — excluding the re-ranking layer, a second component priced separately below. She fixed one loaded engineering cost of ₹2.40 lakh an engineer-month: salary, benefits, employer contributions, equipment and the share of managers and recruiters an engineer consumes. Marketing, sales and support were excluded as identical; revenue effects were handled separately. Because the vendor prices on volume, the volume path came first. From 3.00 crore queries in month one, compounding at 3.5 per cent a month, month 36 carries 3.00 × 1.03535 = 10.00 crore; the 36 terms sum to 210.02 crore, of which 43.81 crore fall in year one, 66.19 crore in year two and 100.02 crore in year three.

The third expert move is pricing the exit. Williamson's hold-up has a rupee value: the cost of leaving. Nirupama estimated one for each option — build, ₹0, though the team is the hostage; buy, data extraction and re-indexing plus the termination fee; open source, the fork she would maintain if the project's governance changed; partner, changing search behaviour under 1,100 live storefronts. Exhibit 3 carries none of them, and a conventional cost of ownership would omit them too, which flatters the columns whose switching costs are largest: partner, whose exit is visible on every storefront, and buy, whose exit is at least contractually enumerable.

4When the framing applies, and when it misleads

Claim one: the component has a definable interface. If you cannot write it in a paragraph, the four-box question is premature. Vedhan's index passes: query in, ranked set out. Vriksha's intake fails as a whole and passes when decomposed — "document capture" has a clean interface, "underwriting judgement" does not.

Claim two: a thick market exists. Buying needs at least three credible suppliers; with one you are not buying, you are being granted terms. Vedhan passes — managed search is competitive, with Algolia, Elastic Cloud and others. Vriksha passes for capture and fails for anything touching Indian life-underwriting rules, where the supplier set is thin and each supplier also serves its competitors.

Claim three: the asset is not specific to you. Vedhan's ranking model trained on merchants' click data is specific; the inverted index beneath it is not — the asymmetry the four-box framing hides. Vriksha splits the same way: optical capture of a bank statement is identical for every insurer in India, while extraction tuned on Vriksha's claims history is worthless to anyone else.

Claim four: the decision is reversible at a price you would pay. Vedhan's vendor index passes — exit is a re-index, which Nirupama priced and would pay. Vriksha's partnered capture passes, reversible inside a quarter. Vriksha's built underwriting rules fail: no price would make the firm unwind its own risk model mid-book, which is why Nachiket moved that component from procurement to a board-level architecture decision.

The framing actively misleads in three situations. First, when the component is the source of a proprietary data asset: buying it gives the supplier the labels, and the supplier's next customer gets the benefit of your volume. Second, when the real constraint is attention rather than money — a 12-person startup that "saves" ₹40 lakh by building has spent its only scarce resource. Third, when a regulator has already decided, as with Vriksha's identity verification below.

5Hard edge cases and the organisational seams

In multi-product firms the decision is taken once and inherited many times. A payments component bought for product A becomes the standard for B and C, never priced into the contract; the volume tier is breached in month 14 and the renewal arrives with the leverage reversed. Mature firms answer with an internal platform team that owns the contract and resells at a transfer price — described as governance, and really a hedge against inheritance.

In two-sided businesses the mode changes the shape of the network. A marketplace that partners for search hands over both sides' behaviour at once, and the partner's business model is to pool it across its customers. Vedhan is a hosted-storefront vendor rather than a marketplace, so the exposure is narrower but real: the partner would see the queries and clicks of 1,100 merchants' shoppers and could use them for the merchants of Vedhan's competitors.

In regulated firms the mode changes who executes and, in India, mostly not who is accountable. The IRDAI's outsourcing framework and the Reserve Bank's 2023 directions on outsourcing of information technology services share a logic: the regulated entity remains responsible, must register material arrangements, must retain inspection and audit rights, and must hold a tested exit plan. Partnering therefore does not remove Vriksha's risk; it converts execution risk into oversight risk. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 adds a layer: Vriksha is the data fiduciary in every mode, and a processor's certification does not transfer that status.

In hardware-plus-software products the two clocks dominate. A component you can change in a sprint and one you can change at the next tooling cycle cannot be sourced on the same logic; buy or partner where the hardware clock governs, and keep in-house the software that compensates for the hardware's limits.

In AI-native products the four boxes have become seven — train, fine-tune, prompt a hosted frontier model, self-host an open-weight model, distil your own small model, buy an application wrapping someone else's model, or partner for the data. The common error is to treat the model as the component. The model is the least specific asset in the stack; the evaluation set, the labelled error taxonomy and the feedback loop are the specific ones, and those are built or they do not exist.

At the organisational seams, what firms do differs from what they say. They say they have a build-versus-buy policy with a threshold. What they have is a procurement process that makes buying slow and a headcount process that makes building slow, and teams route around whichever is slower that quarter. Ask a team that recently built something whether the vendor evaluation would have taken longer; if yes, the policy is a queue.

6Eight nuances that separate the expert

One: the unit is the component, not the capability. The tell is a memo with four options and one verb — "we will build search" rather than "self-host the index, buy the crawler, build the ranker". A decomposed stack almost never resolves to a single mode; Vedhan's resolved to two, and the second, worth ₹158.40 lakh, was invisible until Nikhil named it. Decomposition is not detail to add later. It is the decision; everything after is procurement.

Two: a one-off set against a recurring cost is the commonest arithmetic error in the field. The tell is a build column with a construction estimate and no operating line, beside a buy column carrying three years of subscription. Vedhan's build column is ₹129.60 lakh of construction and ₹162.00 lakh of operation; omitting the operation would have shown build at ₹244.80 lakh — below buy's ₹321.60 lakh and open source's ₹349.20 lakh, within ₹13.80 lakh of partner, and enough to invert the recommendation. It survives in sophisticated firms because construction is a project and operation is somebody's headcount, budgeted separately.

Three: open source is not a price, it is a transfer of obligation. The tell is an open-source proposal with no named owner for the upgrade path. Vedhan's open-source column carries ₹147.60 lakh of infrastructure against buy's ₹21.60 lakh, because self-hosting means paying for the cluster the vendor amortised across all its customers, plus ₹18.00 lakh of migrations. The saving is the vendor's margin; the cost is the vendor's job.

Four: licences change, and the change is strategic, not legal. The tell is a self-hosting plan citing the current licence without naming who controls it. Practitioners who lived through Elastic's 2021 move from Apache 2.0 to the Server Side Public Licence, MongoDB's earlier SSPL move, HashiCorp's 2023 shift to the Business Source Licence and Redis's 2024 relicensing read a dependency as a governance question first: single-vendor project or foundation, and what a fork would cost. Several owners later added permissive or AGPL options, which is the point rather than a refutation — the licence is the owner's variable. What is permanent is the version you hold.

Five: a revenue share is a tax on success, and must be break-even tested against the plan, not today. The tell is a percentage with no break-even revenue. Vedhan's is ₹43.70 crore nominal, ₹44.01 crore in present value, against a plan of ₹28.60 crore and a bull case of ₹46.20 crore. A variable cost is safer against downside and strictly worse against upside — a trade, not a free lunch.

Six: buying the component that produces your labels is how firms lose a data advantage without noticing. The tell is a contract silent on derived data, or a diagram with the model inside the vendor's box. Vriksha's extracted medical fields, matched later against claims experience, are the mortality-selection signal that distinguishes one life insurer from another. What matters is not ownership of the rows but access to the gradient — who sees the errors, who retrains.

Seven: "we have the team" is a reason to build only when the team's next-best use is worse. The tell is a build recommendation whose justification changes when you ask what those engineers would otherwise ship. At full scope Vedhan's build consumes 187.5 engineer-months against buy's 99.75, a difference of 87.75. Salaried engineers are a scarce input with an opportunity cost, not a sunk cost, and a firm that treats them as sunk builds everything and ships nothing.

Eight: the decision has a half-life. The tell is a sourcing decision with no review date. Christensen's integrate-where-not-good-enough argument predicts drift from build to buy as components commoditise, but the AI stack has produced the reverse: firms that bought conversational interfaces in 2023 found by 2025 that the capability was cheap enough to bring in-house and specific enough to own. A good decision comes with a trigger for revisiting it.

7How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the differentiating components are interaction and ranking; identity, payments, messaging and media delivery are commodities, and the decision is rarely contested. In B2B the picture inverts: integrations are the product, so a firm that buys an integration platform has bought what its customers ask about on every sales call — defensible if the market is thick, dangerous if the integrations carry its domain knowledge. In enterprise sales the customer's procurement constrains your sourcing: a sub-processor added for convenience can fail a security review and cost a seven-figure deal, a cost that belongs in the buy column and never appears there.

On platforms and marketplaces, complementors are a sourcing decision at the ecosystem level — letting third parties build a category is buying it with a different instrument. For hardware the bill of materials imposes a discipline software teams lack: every component has a named supplier, a second source and a qualification cost. For AI products the difference is the evaluation, not the model; a firm that does not own its evaluation set cannot tell whether changing supplier helps, so cannot exercise the option buying was meant to preserve. Where the difference is not real, say so: Exhibit 3's arithmetic is unchanged for an AI component.

By stage: a pre-fit company should buy or borrow almost everything, because its scarcest asset is learning cycles. Early scale is the hardest version — bought components have begun to bind and replacing them is still affordable, and Vedhan's ₹158.40 lakh carve-out is exactly that moment. A late-stage company can afford to build anything and therefore builds too much; its characteristic failure is a portfolio of internal platforms with two users and one maintainer each.

8Three worked examples

Example one: building the right commodity

In 2024 Vedhan built its own payment-reconciliation service rather than buying one. Construction took 22 engineer-months, ₹52.80 lakh at the ₹2.40 lakh rate. Steady-state run cost is ₹0.90 lakh a month: 0.25 of an engineer at ₹0.60 lakh plus ₹0.30 lakh of infrastructure — an operating line, deliberately, because the column is worthless without one. The vendor alternative was priced on settlement volume at ₹4.60 lakh a month. The monthly advantage of building is 4.60 − 0.90 = ₹3.70 lakh, so payback is 52.80 ÷ 3.70 = 14.27 months, reached in month 15. Reconciliation is a commodity and nobody's advantage. Both standard framings say buy — core-competence because this is not core, transaction-cost economics because the asset is unspecific — and both are wrong on the facts. Building won on a stable interface, logic that does not change, and a vendor price scaling with a quantity Vedhan expected to grow. The payback is the argument.

Example two: the option that does not exist

Vriksha's identity verification runs through a licensed KYC user agency at ₹5.90 a verification. At 38,000 proposals a month that is ₹2.24 lakh a month, and over 13,68,000 proposals, ₹80.71 lakh. Nachiket's team costed a build and produced a credible engineering estimate, which was worthless. Aadhaar authentication is open only to licensed entities; the licence can be applied for but not purchased, and the application runs on a multi-quarter regulatory clock rather than an engineering one. The build column is therefore not impossible in principle — it is unavailable inside this horizon, which for a horizon-bounded decision is the same thing. Before costing four options, confirm that four exist.

Example three: where it failed, and what recovery cost

Vistrit Diagnostics, a 94-centre pathology chain, bought a laboratory information system in 2023 on a three-year contract at ₹88.80 lakh a year — ₹7.40 lakh a month — with ₹46.00 lakh of implementation: ₹312.40 lakh committed. In month 19 the supplier was acquired, its roadmap frozen, and two integrations Vistrit's hospital clients depended on deprecated. There was no exit plan, no data-extraction estimate and no second source.

9Failure modes and their early warnings

Sourcing a capability rather than a component shows up as a memo with one verb; ask "what are the five components and the mode for each?"; caught late, a re-architecture. Setting a one-off against a recurring cost shows up as a build column with no run line; ask "what is the steady-state headcount in month 30?"; caught late, the credibility of every later model the team produces. Omitting the integration tax shows up as a buy column with no engineering line; ask "who writes the adapter, and for how long?"; caught late, an unplanned quarter. Pricing open source at zero shows up as an infrastructure line matching the vendor's; ask "which engineer's name is against the next major upgrade?"; caught late, a security incident or a stranded version.

Treating a revenue share as a cost shows up as a percentage with no break-even; ask "at what revenue does this become the expensive option?"; caught late, a renegotiation from weakness, because by then the partner knows the number too. Building to retain a team shows up when the recommendation moves with utilisation; ask "what ships if we do not build this?"; caught late, the roadmap. Signing without an exit price is Vistrit's failure; ask "what does leaving cost, and is it in the contract?"; caught late, ₹158.80 lakh on ₹312.40 lakh committed. Buying the label-generating component shows up in a contract silent on derived data; ask "who sees the errors?"; caught late, an advantage never acquired, which nobody books. Deciding once shows up as the absence of a review date; ask "what would have to change, and when do we look?"; caught late, the compounding gap between your stack and the market's.

10Where experts genuinely disagree

Can a bought component ever be a source of advantage? The resource-based position says no, resting on imitability: any supplier who sells to you will sell to your rival, so the component cannot be rare. The opposing position says the advantage lives in the integration and the data flowing through it, and the test is whether a competitor could reproduce the system. For the first to be wrong, there must be durable advantage in configurations of commodity parts; for the second, those configurations must be reproducible faster than the firm can move. The evidence is mixed.

Is "core" knowable before the fact? Core-competence reasoning is accused, not unfairly, of being post-hoc: firms label what they built as their competence and the label does the explanatory work. The defence is that the test is prospective — is this the component customers would not switch away from? For the critique to be wrong, dated ex-ante declarations would have to predict outcomes; for the defence, they would have to track success no better than chance. Nobody has assembled that sample.

Does partnering reduce risk or relocate it? The reducing view notes that a partner carries execution risk, capital and often the licence, and that a firm with no capability must borrow one. The relocating view, which the Indian framework endorses, notes that accountability does not travel with the work, that incentives diverge precisely when things go wrong, and that a firm which partners never acquires the capability. For the first to be wrong, partnered failures would have to cost the principal as much as owned ones; for the second, regulators and customers would have to accept the supplier as responsible, which in Vriksha's case they demonstrably do not.

Does self-hosting actually cost less? Vedhan's figures say no: ₹349.20 lakh for open source against ₹321.60 lakh for buy, and ₹507.60 lakh against ₹480.00 lakh at full scope, because at Vedhan's utilisation the vendor's amortisation beats its own cluster. The counter-case is that this omits option value — freedom from the vendor's future pricing, never quantified. For the cash case to be wrong, utilisation would have to be higher than firms assume; for the option case, vendors would have to be unable to raise prices at renewal, which licence history contradicts.

Has the AI stack broken the framing? Yes, say those who note that capability is rented by the token, that build can be exercised in an afternoon with an open-weight model, and that the stable unit is the data and the evaluation. No, say those who note that this is what every commoditising layer has looked like, that Exhibit 3's arithmetic is unchanged, and that the worst AI sourcing decisions come from firms who think the old discipline has lapsed. For the first to be wrong, the arithmetic would have to keep selecting the options it selected before; for the second, a component's sourcing mode would have to stop predicting who captures its margin. This page takes no side; the disagreement is left open.

11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this arrives with a two-by-two and a recommendation. Someone who has internalised it arrives with a decomposed component list, a named horizon, one loaded labour rate used in every column, a switching cost against each option, a break-even on anything priced as a share of outcome, and a review date. Nirupama's memo has all six: 36 months from 1 November 2026, ₹2.40 lakh an engineer-month, a ₹43.70 crore break-even, and a ₹158.40 lakh component she was nearly talked out of pricing. Such a person is reluctant to answer the question as asked, because it is almost always asked about a capability. They will have asked who sees the errors, and what the engineers would otherwise ship. And where the arithmetic says one thing and they do another, they say so in one sentence and name the price — which distinguishes a judgement from an evasion.

12What they decided

Nirupama Hazarika chose to buy. Her memo of 28 October 2026 put the managed vendor at ₹480.00 lakh at full scope: ₹321.60 lakh for the index and ₹158.40 lakh for the re-ranking layer Vedhan keeps.   1. Nirupama struck out the partner option on scope, then offered its ₹43.70 crore break-even as a second reason. Is the second reason doing any work, or is it cover for a decision already made on architecture? What would you need to see in her memo to tell?

Concept and elevator pitch
The promise decides which components must be yours; sourcing settled before the concept bets on an unwritten specification.
Build, buy or partner
The three-way form, without the open-source column — for drilling the contracting mechanics and hold-up on their own.
Build, fine-tune or buy the model
The same logic where the component is a model: what is the stable unit of advantage when capability is rented by the token?
Writing a solution hypothesis
A falsifiable claim shows which components are load-bearing for the test and which can be faked — the cheapest decomposition you will ever do.
Ideation: brainstorming, Crazy 8s, HMW
Divergent methods generate the alternatives a comparison needs; four columns with one candidate each is a decision already made.
Value Proposition Canvas
Maps the jobs, pains and gains the product is paid for — the only defensible ex-ante test of what counts as core.
Value proposition statement
Forces the promise into one sentence; components absent from it are candidates for buying, and noticing that is most of the skill.
Storyboarding
Reveals the seams a user will experience, and bought or partnered components fail at the seams — where the integration tax lands.
Wireframes, mockups, prototypes
A prototype of bought parts answers the learning question in weeks and commits nothing, which is why the prototype-critique-revise cycle should precede the sourcing decision.

exp20v2-sol.buy.build:
Build, buy, partner or open source

Deciding what must be yours before you design it

1. A Monday in October

On Monday 5 October 2026, Mallika Gadgil, head of product at Tarkash Commerce, opened a one-page memo that her chief technology officer, Madhav Gokhale, had left in the shared folder. Tarkash, based in Pune, sells order-management software to roughly 1,800 small online sellers. A growing share of its customers had crossed that threshold, and they had asked, with growing insistence, for a feature the company did not yet have: automatic generation of GST e-invoices and reconciliation of those invoices against the returns filed with the tax authority. Sellers above the ₹5 crore turnover threshold must report each invoice to the government's Invoice Registration Portal, and a seller who gets this wrong faces blocked invoices and delayed input tax credit.

Madhav's memo said, in one line, that his four best engineers could build the module in nine months. Mohit Gidwani, the finance lead, had attached a second note: a vendor that already ran an e-invoicing service would integrate in three months for a monthly fee plus a charge per invoice. The board meeting was on 30 October. Two of the largest customers had said they would reassess their contracts if the feature was not live by mid-2027, and a competitor had already announced a similar capability.

Mallika's difficulty was not arithmetic alone. If Tarkash built, it would own a capability it might never be able to differentiate, because every competitor must follow the same government specification. If it bought, it would hand a vendor a seat inside its product and a slice of each customer's invoices. The decision had a deadline, a price and a long tail of consequences. This page follows the reasoning she used, because the reasoning, not the answer, is what transfers to other products.

2. The idea

Build, buy, partner or open source is the decision of how to obtain each capability a product needs. To build is to have your own people write and then keep running the capability. To buy is to license it from a vendor, usually through an interface (an API, the agreed way one program asks another to do something) and for a recurring fee. To partner is to have another firm deliver the capability to your customers under a shared commercial arrangement, such as a revenue share, often with the partner's name visible. To use open source is to take software whose source code is published under a licence that permits reuse, and then run, adapt and maintain it yourself.

The problem it solves is an old one in manufacturing, where a firm must decide which parts to make in its own plant and which to purchase. The economist Ronald Coase, in 1937, argued that firms exist because using the market has costs, and that a firm should do an activity internally only when doing so is cheaper than transacting for it. Oliver Williamson refined this from the 1970s into what is called transaction cost economics. Software teams inherited the question when cloud services and open-source libraries made nearly every component purchasable by the early 2010s.

The sentence Mallika could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib is this: we build what makes customers choose us, we buy what customers merely expect, and we decide the rest by comparing total cost over one stated horizon. The first clause is a strategic judgement, the second a market observation and the third an arithmetic exercise. Most confusion in practice comes from letting one of these stand in for another.

3. How it actually works

The method has five steps, and the first is the one practitioners usually leave implicit: define the capability narrowly enough to be compared. "E-invoicing" is not one capability. Mallika split it into generating a valid invoice record, transmitting it to the government portal, receiving the registration number, and reconciling against filed returns. A vendor may cover the first three well and the fourth poorly, so the unit being bought or built must be fixed before any price is compared.

The second step asks whether the capability is a source of differentiation, meaning something customers would cite as the reason they chose you over a rival. The third asks how mature the supply is, that is, whether vendors or open-source projects already do the job to a standard you would accept. Placing the capability on those two axes gives a first answer, drawn in the figure below.

The fourth step is the one that consumes the time: fix a horizon, a scope and a team, then total every cost on that basis. The fifth step lists what could change the answer and assigns each a trigger: a volume threshold, a price rise, a change in the vendor's ownership. Mallika placed e-invoicing in the lower right of the figure, because the specification is set by the government, every seller above the ₹5 crore threshold must comply with it, and several vendors had run it for years. That placement did not settle the matter. It told her the decision was now mostly about money and risk.

4. A worked example

Mallika and Mohit set the horizon at 36 months, from November 2026 to October 2029. Scope: the four-part e-invoicing capability above, for Tarkash's own customers. Team: engineers priced at a loaded cost of ₹2.5 lakh per engineer per month (salary plus overheads). All figures are in ₹ lakh, with 1 crore equal to 100 lakh. Revenue is excluded from both sides, so the comparison covers cost only.

For build, Madhav proposed four engineers for nine months, then one engineer for maintenance during the 27 months of live service, and cloud hosting of ₹0.5 lakh a month once live. For buy, integration would take two engineers three months; the vendor would charge ₹1.2 lakh a month plus ₹0.50 per invoice; and half an engineer would keep the integration healthy during the 33 months of live service. Tarkash expected 60,000 invoices a month, and the table holds that volume constant across every live month.

5. Nuances that separate users from understanders

Cost is not the whole answer

The worked example compares cost only, and it is silent on strategy. Had the capability sat in the top-left of Figure 1, a cheaper vendor would still be the wrong choice. Arithmetic ranks options that are already strategically acceptable; it cannot admit an option that is not.

One-off and recurring costs are different animals

Build is front-loaded and buy is spread across time. A comparison over twelve months favours buy, because build has barely begun to pay back; in general a long enough horizon can favour build, where its running cost per live month is lower than the vendor's. That does not happen with these numbers: build costs 3.0 lakh per live month (2.5 + 0.5) against buy's 2.75 (1.2 + 0.3 + 1.25), so over 120 months build would total 90 + 3.0 × 111 = 423.0 against buy's 15 + 2.75 × 117 = 336.75. Neither horizon is wrong, but the horizon must be stated and held constant. The hidden version of this error is comparing a build cost that stops at launch with a buy cost that runs on.

Build includes keeping it alive

Writing the code is the minority of the lifetime effort. Regulation changes, portals change their formats, and bugs surface. Madhav's single maintenance engineer is the largest line in the build column after construction, and it is the line most often forgotten.

Buying does not remove engineering

The buy column still carries ₹41.25 lakh of engineering upkeep, because someone must monitor the integration, handle the vendor's failures and map its data to Tarkash's. A vendor shifts the work; it does not delete it.

Partnering is a different thing from buying

A purchase leaves the customer relationship with you. A partnership usually shares it: the partner may bill the customer, appear in the interface or hold the data. That can be acceptable for a peripheral capability and dangerous for a central one. The cheapest sign is who the customer sends the complaint to.

Open source is free to obtain and costly to own

An open-source component carries no licence fee, but you inherit its maintenance, security patches and, depending on the licence, obligations. Permissive licences (such as MIT or Apache 2.0) let you embed the code in a commercial product, but they still require you to keep the licence and copyright notices, and Apache 2.0 adds an express patent grant and a NOTICE file. "Copyleft" licences require more: the GNU AGPL obliges anyone who modifies the software and lets users interact with it over a network to offer those users the corresponding source code, which is precisely the situation of a software-as-a-service company like Tarkash. Treat it as a build with a head start, and have a lawyer read the licence.

Reversibility is a cost

Switching away from a vendor, or from your own code, has a price. Ask what it would take to leave in month 18: is the data exportable, are contracts annual, is the interface standard? A lower headline cost with high lock-in is often a worse option than a higher cost with an exit.

The numbers are forecasts

The nine-month estimate, the volume and the vendor's pricing are all uncertain. Engineering estimates for new work tend to run long. The useful practice is to ask which input, if wrong by a factor of two, would flip the answer, as the second pass did for volume.

6. How it differs by product type and by stage

In consumer products, the experience is the differentiator, so teams build what shapes the feel of the product and buy the plumbing: payments, messaging, maps. In B2B products such as Tarkash's, integrations and compliance are frequent candidates for buying, since the customer cares that they work and not who wrote them; but data ownership and security reviews weigh heavily. In marketplaces, the matching and trust mechanisms between buyers and sellers are usually the heart of the business and tend to be built, while identity checks, payments and logistics are often bought or partnered.

Stage matters as much. An early-stage company has few engineers, uncertain demand and a short runway, so it should buy aggressively and accept lock-in as the price of speed. A large company has scale that makes per-unit vendor fees expensive, as the break-even at the right of Figure 2 shows, and has the engineers to carry maintenance. The same capability can therefore be rationally bought at one size and built at another. What changes is the volume and the cost of an engineer, not the logic.

Figure 3 lays the two routes on one clock. The horizontal axis counts months from the start of month 1 (November 2026) to the end of month 36 (October 2029), so each boundary is the end of a month. The integration for buy ends at the end of month 3, and its 33 live months run to the end of the horizon. The build ends at the end of month 9, leaving 27 live months. The dashed lines mark those two boundaries. Reading the figure alongside the cost table shows why the totals differ: build pays four engineers for the long first bar, while buy pays a subscription for the long green bar.

7. Common mistakes

Comparing different horizons. The symptom: the build case looks cheap in the slide but a finance reviewer finds its maintenance missing. The misunderstanding is treating launch as the end of cost. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask, for every line, "until when?", and check that both columns end on the same date.

Building because it is interesting. The symptom: a team describes the commodity capability in terms of its elegant architecture. The misunderstanding is mistaking capability for advantage. Diagnostic: ask what a customer would say if the feature were bought, and whether they would notice.

Buying without an exit. The symptom: a renewal arrives and nobody can say what leaving would involve. The misunderstanding is treating the contract as permanent. Diagnostic: write the one-page migration plan before signing, and note how many weeks it takes.

Treating open source as free. The symptom: a component is adopted without an owner, and a security patch sits unapplied for months. The misunderstanding is equating no licence fee with no cost. Diagnostic: name the person who will read the project's release notes each month; if there is none, price one.

8. What good looks like

A well-handled decision begins with a written definition of the capability and its placement on the two axes, with a sentence of justification for each. It states the horizon, scope and team in the first line of the cost table. It separates one-off from recurring cost, shows the working behind every figure, and identifies the single input most likely to flip the answer. It names a trigger, for example "revisit if monthly invoices exceed 4,00,000", and an owner. It records what leaving would take. Finally, it is short enough for a board to read in ten minutes, and the product lead can defend each number without notes.

9. What Mallika decided

On 30 October Mallika recommended buying. The reasoning had three parts. The capability was a commodity with mature supply. On the agreed horizon, buying cost ₹105.75 lakh against ₹171.00 lakh to build, and the answer would not flip unless volume grew to roughly 7.6 times the forecast. And the vendor route would be live in February 2027, about six months earlier than the build route, which protected the two large accounts. She attached conditions: an annual contract with data export, a monthly review of the vendor's error rate, and a trigger to reopen the question if average monthly volume approaches 4,00,000 invoices. She also asked Madhav to keep one engineer's design notes for a possible later build, so that the option stayed alive.

What to learn next: the sibling topics on build, buy or partner as a strategic choice, and on build, fine-tune or buy the model, apply the same logic to machine-learning models, where the supply is less mature and the cost structure differs. Learn them after this page because they reuse its horizon-and-scope discipline.

Two questions to sit with. First, which capability in a product you know well would you currently describe as core, and would a customer agree with you? Second, if the vendor doubled its per-invoice charge, which single line of your cost table would you re-examine first, and why?
case20v1-sol.buy.build:
Bandhu Stores Technologies: What Must We Build Ourselves?

A teaching case on build, buy, partner or open source

1. Opening

On the morning of Monday, 19 October 2026, Irshad Mehendale, founder and chief executive of Bandhu Stores Technologies, sat in the Andheri East office in Mumbai with a one-page note and two dates circled on it. The board would meet on Friday, 6 November. A week later, on Friday, 13 November, the price quoted by a lending-software vendor, Bodhi Lending Systems, would lapse.

Bandhu had decided, after a year of retailer requests, to launch a working-capital credit line inside its ordering app. The launch was settled. How much of the machinery behind it Bandhu should construct itself was not, and each of his senior colleagues pulled toward a different answer.

2. Company background

Bandhu, founded in Mumbai in 2019, runs an ordering app through which owners of kirana stores in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka buy staples and packaged goods from distributors and brand sales teams. In the financial year 2025-26 about 1,10,000 retailers ordered through the app, and gross merchandise value was ₹4,200 crore. Bandhu earns a commission of about 1.8 per cent, which gave net revenue of ₹75.6 crore. It employs 212 people, 38 of them engineers in Pune and Bengaluru.

Udaan, Jumbotail, Flipkart Wholesale and JioMart all court the same shopkeepers, and Khatabook and OkCredit already own the habit of keeping a shop's credit ledger on a phone. Bandhu's edge is not scale but data: fourteen months of order, return and payment-timing history for each retailer.

3. The situation

Since January 2026 Bandhu has offered 15-day pay-later of up to ₹25,000, funded from its own balance sheet. Retailers want more: loans of ₹50,000 to ₹3 lakh over twelve months to stock up before festivals. The proposed product, the Bandhu Capital Line, would be funded by Bharani Finance, an RBI-registered NBFC. Under the RBI's digital lending rules Bandhu would act only as a lending service provider, offering a first-loss guarantee that RBI caps at 5 per cent of the loan portfolio. The finance team forecasts 1,25,000 loans of an average ₹1.2 lakh, or ₹1,500 crore disbursed, over 36 months. That is the horizon used throughout this case: 36 months from kickoff on 1 December 2026 to 30 November 2029.

Every option shares the same NBFC partner, so its terms are outside the comparison. What differs is who supplies five components: credit scoring and decisioning; the loan ledger and servicing; KYC, e-sign and e-mandate; collections and reconciliation; and compliance controls, including those required by the DPDP Act. Exhibit 1 sets out the 36-month cost of three ways to assemble them.

The people most affected saw it differently, from different time zones. In Pune, Indrasen Manjrekar regarded a ledger as plumbing his team could assemble. In Toronto, Indulekha Malpani, who built Bandhu's retailer risk model, worried that a vendor would discard her signals. In Berlin, Ipsita Mukerji feared that a white-label flow would make the loan screen a stranger's product. Berlin sits three and a half to four and a half hours behind Mumbai and Toronto nine and a half to ten and a half, so Mumbai's afternoon decisions reached Toronto only as her morning began.

4. The people

Irshad Mehendale, Mumbai. Founder and chief executive. He wants the credit line live before the 2027 festive season, when kirana restocking peaks, and a recommendation the board will find defensible.

Indrasen Manjrekar, Pune. Head of engineering. He favours building everything, to guard against vendor price rises, though no one on his team has run a lending ledger.

Indulekha Malpani, Toronto. Data scientist. She wants her order-data model to make every credit decision, and cites Exhibit 2 as proof.

Ipsita Mukerji, Berlin. Senior designer. She wants to own the offer, repayment and reminder screens, because retailers who miss a repayment will blame the app they open daily.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 puts Option A at ₹8.8 crore, B at ₹4.8 crore and C at ₹5.8 crore. C costs ₹1.0 crore more than B, which spread across ₹1,500 crore of disbursals is about 0.07 per cent. Exhibit 2 tests what the scoring model delivers.

Between January and June 2026, 6,400 retailers opened pay-later accounts, none used to build Malpani's model. Bodhi's standard model, which uses bureau, GST and bank-statement data, and Malpani's model, which uses fourteen months of order, return and payment-timing data alongside the bureau file, each ranked the 6,400 and each approved its top 70 per cent.

Bandhu's model produced 112 fewer delinquent accounts among the approved, a gap of 2.5 percentage points. Bandhu's finance lead cautioned, correctly, that the test measured short pay-later balances, not twelve-month loans of ₹1.2 lakh, so it cannot be converted into write-offs. Nor can it say which of Malpani's inputs does the work. It shows only that the models rank Bandhu's own customers differently.

Exhibit 3 adds time: B is live by 1 May 2027, C by 1 September 2027 and A by 1 February 2028, after the festive season.

6. The options

Option A: build everything. Bandhu writes its own scoring, ledger, collections and integrations. Total cost is ₹8.8 crore, or ₹704 a loan, and the company owns every screen and every rule. The upside is control and no vendor fees; the cost is the highest total, the longest wait, and a ledger built by engineers who have never run one.

Option B: buy Bodhi's platform. Bodhi supplies scoring, ledger, KYC and collections as one package, configured for Bandhu. Total cost is ₹4.8 crore, or ₹384 a loan, with a live date in May 2027. The upside is speed and a proven ledger. The cost is a generic model that did worse in Exhibit 2, limited control of the repayment screens, and dependence on one vendor. Bodhi has said it could retrain on Bandhu's order data after six months, for a fee not yet quoted.

Option C: build the scoring, borrow the rest. Bandhu builds the scoring and decisioning layer on Malpani's model, runs Apache Fineract as the ledger, and buys KYC and e-sign as pay-per-use APIs. Total cost is ₹5.8 crore, or ₹464 a loan, live in September 2027. The upside is owning the one component built on Bandhu's data. The cost is ₹1.0 crore more than B, a team that must learn to operate open-source software, and a launch four months after B.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Which components in Exhibit 1 could a competitor such as Udaan or Jumbotail copy within a year, and which could it not? What does that imply for Bandhu's engineering time?

2. What does Exhibit 2 establish, and what can it not? What further measurement would you ask Malpani for before relying on it for twelve-month loans?

3. Option C costs ₹1.0 crore more than B over 36 months. What improvement in write-offs, as a share of ₹1,500 crore disbursed, would justify it, and what must be true about the four months of delay in Exhibit 3?

4. Which option would you take to the board on 6 November, with what checkpoint, and what would make you switch?

8. A note for the learner

This topic frames the choice as a question to ask before designing anything: what must be ours, and what can we buy or borrow? A useful rule has three tests. Build a component if it is the source of advantage, if evidence shows Bandhu does it better, and if the extra cost is small against what it protects. Buy or borrow the rest, using open source where Bandhu can operate it safely. Partner where regulation requires it, which is why Bharani Finance sits in every option.

Applying the tests: scoring is the advantage, because it runs on data only Bandhu holds, and Exhibit 2 is the evidence, within its limits. The premium is a low bar: ₹1.0 crore over ₹1,500 crore of disbursals is about 0.07 per cent. Whether Bandhu's model clears it is not shown, since Exhibit 2 cannot be converted into write-offs on twelve-month loans. The ledger, KYC and e-sign are commodities that other lenders run identically. Option A builds commodities as well as the advantage, and misses the festive season. Option B wins on speed but gives away the one component the evidence favours.

One defensible path is Option C, with conditions. Ask Bodhi to extend its quote by 90 days, to 11 February 2027, so Option B stays as a fallback. Set a checkpoint on 1 February 2027, inside that window: if Malpani's model has not held up on fresh pay-later accounts opened July to September 2026 and observed to 31 January, or Manjrekar's team has not stood up the Fineract ledger in a test environment, switch to Bodhi and negotiate the retraining clause. A switch then means a five-month start from 1 February, live about 1 July 2027, two months later than Exhibit 3 shows for B. Give Mukerji the screens either way. The weak point is the 1 September date, which rests on a team that has not run a ledger before; a good answer says so.

Mandhira Supply Technologies: What Must Be Ours to Build?

A routing engine, four ways to get one, and a board meeting in the morning.

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on the night of Tuesday, 27 October 2026, Tarini Bhide was still at the office on Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru. On the table were four printouts, each a thirty-six-month cost of a routing engine, and a note from the chief financial officer fixing the programme envelope at ₹7.5 crore. Three of the four fitted inside it. By her own arithmetic, done that evening on the back of the fourth, none did.

The board of Mandhira Supply Technologies met at nine the next morning in Pune, and the second item was hers: how to route the 54 lakh delivery stops clients had been promised in the coming year. The horizon she had been told to price was the thirty-six months from 1 November 2026 to 31 October 2029, and every number she would show covered exactly that window. What they did not cover was that the four options did not start at the same time, while the plan beneath them assumed all 54 lakh stops routed from month one.

On the Mottram quotation her deputy had left a sticky note: price hold expires 15 November. The Mutlaq renewal was due 31 March 2027. The Coimbatore planning cell, twelve people who drew the routes by hand nightly, had been told in August that a decision was imminent; two had since resigned.

2. How Mandhira came to be constrained

Mandhira was founded in Pune in March 2016 by Tanishq Borkar, who had spent nine years selling distribution software to pharmaceutical wholesalers and concluded the mid-market wanted not an ERP but order-to-doorstep. By September 2026 the platform — order management, warehousing, last-mile fulfilment — had 310 clients, 420 employees across Pune, Bengaluru and Coimbatore, 86 of them in engineering, and ₹46 crore of annual recurring revenue. A Series B of ₹190 crore in March 2025 left ₹88 crore of cash at 30 September 2026.

One decision from that history shaped everything. In February 2023 the board approved an in-house warehouse-management module at ₹96 lakh and eight months, no available product having modelled the loose-case picking pharma distribution requires. It shipped in September 2024, nineteen months later, at ₹240 lakh — 2.5 times the estimate. Borkar still defends it as the reason Mandhira wins pharma accounts. Its cost was not only money. It writes stop sequences, bin references and addresses in a bespoke format no outside system reads, and when Tobias Beaulieu's team in Toronto replayed historical routes through candidate engines in April and May 2026, 212 of the 2,612 routes attempted would not parse. The 2023 decision to build is why every option before the board carries an integration cost.

3. The industry

By 2026 India's last-mile market bought software in two quite different ways. The quick-commerce and food platforms — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy, Zomato — treated dispatch as the core of the company and would no more licence it than licence their pricing. The shippers Mandhira served, mid-market distributors and regional chains, had no such conviction: they wanted on-time delivery, a GST-compliant e-way bill trail and somebody to call at night. Between them sat the logistics majors — Delhivery, Blue Dart, the Mahindra and Reliance Retail fleets — whose dispatch systems were now offered to shippers as a service.

Three forces pressed on the decision. ONDC had taught Mandhira's clients to expect an interoperable fulfilment connector, and four had been promised one by 30 June 2027. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 had made cross-border processing of consignee data a board question, not a procurement footnote, and a September 2026 security review found two clients, both distributing financial products, whose contracts forbade offshore processing of addresses outright, whatever the Act permitted. And the largest customer was not in India: Mutlaq Retail Group, a grocery and pharmacy chain with 310 stores across the UAE and Oman, paid ₹7.4 crore a year — ₹7.4 crore of the ₹52 crore Year 1 plan, or 14.2 per cent — against route plans by 05:30 Gulf Standard Time, 99.5 per cent availability and UAE residency for Emirati consignee data. Breach cost ₹18 lakh a month, capped at ₹1.08 crore.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

Dispatch began in 2019 as a service, not a product: planners in Coimbatore took the day's orders at six in the evening and drew routes in a spreadsheet against a printed map. The cell cost ₹7 lakh a month; volume ended the argument. At the 4.5 lakh stops a month of the Year 1 plan it was finishing at 23:40 on peak nights, and Diwali week of 2025 produced 14 route sets that reached drivers after departure.

In April 2025 Mandhira opened a role for an operations-research engineer. Over two attempts and fourteen months it drew 97 applications, 11 phone screens and 3 offers; two declined, both citing pay, and the one who joined in June 2025 left five months later. The Bengaluru band was ₹48 lakh fully loaded; Beaulieu, who does comparable work in Toronto, costs ₹1.05 crore. Tejasvi Barve read the record as proof that building was impossible; Tishya Bhagat, who had run the 2023 module, read it as proof the company had sought a specialist instead of training the three engineers it had.

Mottram Routing Systems, a Birmingham firm with 140 customers in Europe and six in India, presented in February 2026; its engine is hosted in London by default, with a Mumbai region available and a UAE region that exists for exactly the reason Mutlaq cares about. In June 2026, after Mandhira lost two mid-market deals to a shipper portal run by Mehroz Express — a ₹4,100 crore Indian third-party logistics firm with 240 hubs — Mehroz proposed that Mandhira white-label its dispatch engine for 8 per cent of routed-account revenue, on five-year India exclusivity with a most-favoured-nation clause. Two of Bhagat's engineers had, unasked, assembled a prototype on Google OR-Tools and OSRM over six weekends in February and March 2026, hence its row in the replay. It routed. Procurement at three enterprise clients then asked whom Mandhira would name as supported vendor, which is how Maitreya Open Systems, a 40-engineer Bengaluru consultancy, came to quote ₹3 lakh a month for support.

Two beliefs of that period have turned out wrong. The first was that the April–May replay (Exhibit 4) had settled engine quality; the pilot that followed (Exhibit 5) measured a different thing in different cities. The second was that the ₹7.5 crore envelope was generous. 5. The people

Tarini Bhide — vice-president, product, Bengaluru. Owns the recommendation; will not recommend what the company cannot staff. Incentive: an ONDC connector promised to four clients by 30 June 2027, which Option A would strip of six engineers. Unsaid: she wrote the note Exhibit 3 was built from, now thinks it misled the board, and has not told Bhavnani.

Tanishq Borkar — co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Routing is the heart of the platform, and a company that rents its heart is a reseller at renewal. Incentive: a Series C pitch in which “proprietary dispatch intelligence” is a slide. Unsaid: he approved the 2023 estimate himself, and a July 2026 investor memo called that module “capital spent on undifferentiated plumbing”.

Tejasvi Barve — chief technology officer, Bengaluru. Wants to buy; says the hiring record settles it. Incentive: the 99.5 per cent availability the Mutlaq contract makes contractual. Unsaid: Mottram has offered to second two engineers to Bengaluru for a year, easing the hiring problem under any option.

Tishya Bhagat — director of engineering, Pune. Holds that the 2023 overrun was a specification, not an engineering, failure, and that her engineers' weekend prototype came within two points of Mottram on the replay. Unsaid: both have interviewed elsewhere this year, and the prototype has never carried a peak evening.

Trupti Bhavnani — chief financial officer, Pune. Set the envelope, and cut the replay's ₹14.75 a stop to ₹6.20 on the view that replayed routes assume a rider compliance the field never delivers. Prefers D on cash. Incentive: a 68 per cent gross-margin commitment for Year 2. Unsaid: five-year exclusivity is what diligence calls an encumbrance.

Tobias Beaulieu — principal data scientist, Toronto. Built the replay and refuses to rank engines on it: replay and pilot measure different things in different cities, and nothing is known about the stack under peak load. Unsaid: he believes the lock-in sits in the map and travel-time data, not the solver.

Ting-Wei Bok — director of customer success, Singapore. Carries the escalations, including Diwali 2025's 14 late route sets, and wants whichever option is live soonest: C. Incentive: nine enterprise renewals. Unsaid: two of those clients have asked whether Mandhira is becoming a front end for Mehroz.

Trent Bellamy — senior vice-president, sales, New Jersey. Wants Mottram, and cites Exhibit 5's 11.1-point on-time gap everywhere. Incentive: a US pipeline where a named engine with SOC 2 shortens security review by weeks. Unsaid: his largest prospect is a Mottram reference customer and has already seen the Dubai figures.

6. Where the work actually sits

Beaulieu's objection is to the framing, and is clearest in the layering he drew on a whiteboard in August. The engine is not one thing. The dispatch workflow, the constraint model encoding a client's service promises, the solver, the map and travel-time data it reasons over, and the telemetry that closes the loop are five separable layers, and each option is a bundle of five decisions. Mottram sells layers two to four as one product; Mehroz supplies three and four and insists on its own layer two; the open-source stack gives away three and four at a quality he thinks poor on interior roads, where Mandhira's own 2.1 crore stop timestamps beat any public extract.

8. The options as Bhide sees them

A. Build in-house. Six engineers for ten months, live in month 11, nothing owed to anybody: ₹643 lakh in Exhibit 3, ₹921.8 lakh comparable. It costs the ONDC commitment, and its estimate is the one the company has least right to believe.

B. Buy Mottram. Live in month 4, SOC 2 in hand, a UAE region that satisfies Baroudi: ₹972.6 lakh comparable, or ₹1,111.2 lakh if the two clients forbidding offshore processing require the Mumbai region.

C. Partner with Mehroz. Live in month 2, ₹763.9 lakh comparable, second only to D, and the only option that worsens the better Mandhira sells: 8 per cent of routed revenue, five-year exclusivity, most-favoured-nation.

D. Open source. ₹752.2 lakh comparable, the lowest of the four, and, like A, it keeps constraint model, solver and telemetry inside the company. It depends on hiring Mandhira has twice failed at, on two engineers who have been interviewing, and on a stack nobody has run through a Diwali.

Bhide's unease is not with any of the four. It is that she has written them as four, when Exhibit 3's footnotes break those four into separate cost lines and Figure 1 describes five layers. Nothing in the Mottram contract stops Mandhira keeping layer two, nor the open-source licences its licensing a travel-time matrix where OSRM is weakest. Nothing but the shape of the board paper requires a one-word answer.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at nine on Wednesday, 28 October 2026 and expects a recommendation. Money: ₹750 lakh approved, and all four comparable figures in Exhibit 6 exceed it — the nearest by ₹2.2 lakh, the farthest by ₹222.6 lakh. People: fourteen net engineering heads against 86 today, and Option A needs six redeployed from ONDC work promised for 30 June 2027. Regulation: the DPDP Act permits the transfer, two client contracts do not, and Mutlaq requires UAE residency whoever supplies the engine. Contracts: Mottram's term runs thirty-six months with no exit before month 24; Mehroz's exclusivity five years, longer than the horizon priced. Time: the Mutlaq renewal falls in month 5, and only B and C are live before it.

At midnight Bhide wrote three words at the top of her working sheet — what must be ours — and under them the only sentence she was sure of: that the Coimbatore cell would draw tomorrow evening's routes by hand whatever the board decided, and keep doing so for somewhere between one month and ten. She turned off the lamp without deciding which.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. State the basis on which Exhibit 3 compares the four options, and what must be added before any two of its figures can be compared.
  2. Exhibits 4 and 5 point in different directions about the open-source prototype. What does each measure, over what base, and what can neither answer?
  3. Bhavnani cut the replay's ₹14.75 a stop to ₹6.20. Is that defensible, what would move it, and which option does it most affect?
  4. The 2023 module cost 2.5 times its estimate and is why 212 routes would not parse. How much weight should that overrun carry against a 2026 estimate, and how would you decide it?
  5. Take Figure 1 seriously and build a fifth option across the five layers. Price it over the horizon, name the layer you would not give up on any terms, and say what evidence would change your mind.
  6. It is Monday morning, 2 November 2026, and the board wants Bhide back in a fortnight with one recommendation and one number. What does she do first, what does she stop doing to make room, and what does she say to a board already shown a ₹750 lakh envelope?
